text.hook:
std::visit is not resolved at compile time.
And a variant can end up holding nothing.

The mental model for variant and any, plus 6 myths. Swipe ➜
text.body:
Inside:
1. Closed set vs open set
2. Size and construction rules
3. visit vs virtual functions
4. monostate vs valueless_by_exception
5. std::any rules
6. Six myths, busted (slides 8-9)

Which myth did you believe? Comment the slide number.

slides.lead: A tagged union that knows its type, a type-erased box, and when to use neither.

slides.title: Closed set or open set?

cards.label: variant<A, B, C> (C++17)
cards.text: Exactly one of a **fixed** list of types. Stored in place, plus an index.

cards.label: any (C++17)
cards.text: One object of any copyable type, decided at run time. Ask for the exact type back.

cards.label: Virtual functions
cards.text: Types added later by other modules, with common behaviour.

slides.takeaway: All known where you declare it: `variant`. Extended later: a virtual interface. Payload you never inspect: `any`.

slides.title: Largest alternative + an index
slides.takeaway: The variant never allocates by itself. One huge alternative makes every element huge.

slides.title: Which alternative do you get?
rows: The string (P0608, C++20 DR, GCC 10+). Older libraries: `true`

slides.title: Two kinds of dispatch
rows: Visitors with no viable handler fail to compile / old code untouched
Write one new visitor / new virtual in every class
slides.takeaway: `visit` branches on the run-time index (no vptr). The usual win is memory layout, not the dispatch instruction.

slides.title: monostate vs valueless

cards.label: std::monostate
cards.text: Deliberate: "nothing yet". Put it first so the variant is default-constructible.

cards.label: valueless_by_exception
cards.text: Accidental: the old alternative was destroyed, then the new one's construction threw.

slides.takeaway: Make alternatives nothrow-move-constructible. Assigning a new value recovers the variant.

slides.title: Rules that surprise people
items: Copy-constructible types only: a `unique_ptr` does not compile
By-value `any_cast<T>(a)` copies the object: use `any_cast<T&>` or the pointer form for big ones
Copying an `any` deep-copies the held object: it is never shared
libstdc++ stores only pointer-sized, nothrow-movable types inline: a `std::string` allocates
No compile-time checks: every access is a run-time type comparison

items.myth: "`std::variant` allocates the alternative on the heap."
items.truth: It lives in place. Size is the largest alternative plus an index.
It branches on the run-time index. The handlers can be inlined.
It tracks the active type, runs the right constructors and destructors, and checks access.
It can be valueless after a throwing alternative change.

items.myth: "`get<T>` returns nullptr on the wrong type."
"`variant` is always faster than virtual functions."
items.truth: It wins on layout and allocation. Dispatch cost is similar.

slides.hero:
Closed set: variant.
Open set: virtual.
Opaque payload: any.
slides.lead: Save this. Follow for a C++ interview puzzle every day.

text.hook:
The visitor has no `double` handler.
The variant holds 101.75.
Does std::visit catch the gap?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body:
std::visit promises exhaustiveness. What exactly does it check?
C++20 (aggregate CTAD). In C++17, add the usual `overloaded` deduction guide.

slides.title: No double handler. What prints?

bullets: `visit` checks that the visitor is **callable** with every alternative.
It is: overload resolution converts `double` to `int`.
The `int` lambda runs and 101.75 is truncated to 101.
The conversion happens inside the library, so no warning fires.
slides.wrong: "A: a missing alternative is always a compile error"

slides.title: Handle it, and forbid fallbacks
slides.tip: Remove the `double` lambda now and the `static_assert` fires: the catch-all accepts only types with no exact handler.
slides.takeaway: Exhaustiveness in `visit` means "callable with". Implicit conversions count.

text.hook:
A reference into a variant holding 42.
Then the variant gets a new value.
Same storage, same address.

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.

slides.title:
Is this well-defined?
What does it print?
options: UB: qty refers to a dead int

slides.verdict_sub: GCC 11, `-O0`: a different number each run. ASan: silent
bullets: Assigning a `std::string` **destroys** the `int` and constructs a string in the same storage.
`qty` now points at bytes of the string object (libstdc++: part of its data pointer).
Writing through `qty` would corrupt the string and crash later in its destructor.
`field = 7;` would have been fine: same alternative, plain assignment.
slides.wrong: "A: the storage is still there, so the reference is fine"

slides.title: Copy the value out, re-fetch later
slides.takeaway: A reference into a variant is valid only while that alternative stays active.

text.hook:
A slot that is empty until the first order arrives.
`std::variant<Order, std::string> slot;`
What could go wrong?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Order has one explicit constructor taking an int.

slides.title:
Does this compile?
If yes, what does it print?

bullets: A default-constructed variant holds a value-initialized **first** alternative.
`Order` has no default constructor, so the variant's default constructor is deleted.
A variant is never "empty by default".
Even with a default `Order`, a fake order is a poor initial state.

slides.title: Make "nothing yet" explicit
slides.takeaway: The first alternative decides default construction. Use `std::monostate` for an explicit empty state.

text.hook:
`std::any a = 42;`
Ask for a `long`, an `int`, an `unsigned`.
All integers. All should work. Right?

Lock in your answer below, then swipe ➜ to verify.
text.body: Pointer form and value form of any_cast fail in different ways.

slides.title: What does it print?

slides.verdict_sub: Only the exact stored type matches
bullets: The check is a `type_info` comparison. No promotions, no conversions.

slides.title: Decay happens on the way in
slides.tip: Store `std::string("hello")` if readers will ask for a `std::string`.
slides.takeaway: `any_cast` matches the exact stored type. There are no conversions.
